title: Australia Slows Working Holiday Visa Processing, Pauses Applications From 24 Countries
excerpt: High application volumes have triggered longer processing times and widespread pauses for subclass 462 visas. India and China face a separate ballot process.
body:
• Australia has slowed processing of Working Holiday Maker visas amid high application volumes since July 2026
  • First Work and Holiday (subclass 462) visa applications have been paused for 24 capped partner countries
  • India, China and Vietnam face a separate ballot process rather than direct applications
  • Application fees have increased to AUD 840 for first visas, up from AUD 670

Australia's Working Holiday Maker program is facing significant disruption as the Department of Home Affairs slows visa processing and pauses first applications from 24 countries under the Work and Holiday (subclass 462) stream, affecting young workers and the businesses that rely on them.

What Changed

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke confirmed on August 16 that Working Holiday visas continue to be processed, but "more slowly than they were previously," with no revised timeframe announced. The department attributed the delays to high volumes of applications received since the July 1 start of the 2026-27 program year.

For the subclass 462 stream, which is subject to annual country caps, applications from 24 countries have been paused, including Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Spain and Thailand. During a pause, nationals of affected countries cannot lodge new first visa applications, though second and third visa applications remain unaffected.

Impact on Indian Applicants

India, China and Vietnam use a separate ballot process for Working Holiday visas rather than the standard application stream. While the pause does not directly affect Indian applicants in the same way, the broader processing slowdown applies to all Working Holiday Maker visa subclasses, including the subclass 417 stream used by applicants from countries like the UK, Germany and Denmark.

Reports indicate that some applicants from subclass 417 countries have been waiting nearly six weeks for approval since July 1, compared to the near-instant processing that was previously common.

Economic Consequences

The Tourism and Transport Forum warned that the delays are putting tourism businesses, regional economies and future visitor demand at risk. Working Holiday Makers spent approximately AUD 1.1 billion in regional Australia in 2025 and AUD 3.3 billion in capital cities, according to Tourism Research Australia data.

"Working Holiday Makers are not simply temporary workers. They are high-value, long-stay international visitors who work, travel and spend across Australia."

— Margy Osmond, CEO, Tourism & Transport Forum

Agricultural businesses are particularly concerned, with harvest season approaching and visa delays threatening to create worker shortages during critical periods.

Fee Increases

Since July 1, the fee for a first Working Holiday visa application has increased to AUD 840, up from AUD 670. Second and third applications now cost AUD 1,000, adding to the financial burden on prospective applicants.

What's Next

The department says paused country caps are expected to reopen later in the same program year. Applicants need to monitor the Home Affairs website for status changes. The situation reflects broader migration policy settings under the Australian government's effort to manage net migration numbers.
